# Introduction

## The Cappuccino Index

James Hoffmann is a YouTuber who explores coffee from many different angles. In a recent [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WtlE3BW9Nqs) he explored how long a barista would need to work to pay for a small cappuccino.

> Coffee, as a part of our economy, as an industry, is full of these awkward questions that I do think are worth asking.

In the video, James presents the cappuccino index, which answers this at a country level. 

There are some important caveats, such as tips being excluded.

[Data Source & Description](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/blob/main/data/2026/2026-09-08/readme.md)


## Data Dictionary - `cafe`

|variable          |class     |description                           |
|:-----------------|:---------|:-------------------------------------|
|country           |character |The country of the cafe. |
|city              |character |The city of the cafe. |
|urban             |logical   |Whether the cafe is in an urban area. |
|suburban          |logical   |Whether the cafe is in a suburban area. |
|rural             |logical   |Whether the cafe is in a rural area. |
|hourly_wage_gbp   |double    |The hourly wage of a barista working in the cafe, converted to British pounds. |
|price_gbp         |double    |The price of a small cappuccino from the cafe, converted to British pounds. |
|original_currency |character |The original currency used by the cafe. |
|price             |double    |The price of a small cappuccino from the cafe, in the original currency. |
|hourly_wage       |double    |The hourly wage of a barista working in the cafe, in the original currency. |


## Data Dictionary - `cappuccino_index`


|variable      |class     |description                           |
|:-------------|:---------|:-------------------------------------|
|country       |character |Name of country for which cappuccino index was calculated. |
|index         |double    |The cappuccino index: the time in minutes a barista needs to work to afford a small cappuccino in their country. |
|n             |integer   |Number of cafes that were included in the calculation of the index. |
|minutes       |double    |The number of whole minutes in index. |
|seconds       |double    |The remaining number of seconds in index. |
|index_as_time |character |Index formatted as minutes and seconds, i.e., MM:SS. |

## Read in the Data


```{r}
#| echo: true
cafe <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-09-08/cafe.csv')
cappuccino_index <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-09-08/cappuccino_index.csv')


cafe$country <- gsub("\u00a0", " ", cafe$country) # <1>
cappuccino_index$country <- gsub("\u00a0", " ", cappuccino_index$country) # <1>
```
1. Replace non-breaking spaces with regular spaces

# Categorical Distributions
## Participating Countries

```{r}
#| echo: true

cafe_plot <- cafe |>
  count(country) |> # <1>
  mutate(prop = n/sum(n)) |> # <2>
  arrange(desc(prop)) |> # <3>
  head(10) # <4> 
cafe_plot <- bind_rows(
  tibble(country = "Other", # <5>
         n = 2594 - sum(cafe_plot$n),  # <5>
         prop = 1-sum(cafe_plot$prop)), # <5>
  cafe_plot) |>
  mutate(country = factor(country, levels = country, ordered = T)) # <6>
  
head(cafe_plot)
```
1.  `count(var)` is a shortcut for `group_by(var) |> summarize(n = n()) |> ungroup()` - it counts up the number of rows with each value of var.
2.  Calculate the proportion from the number of observations with a specific value and total number of observations
3.  Sort the dataset by `desc(prop)`
4.  Take the top 10 rows -- there are too many countries to show
5.  Create an "Other" row that includes everything else
6.  Reorder the levels of country based on decreasing proportion

## Participating Countries

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-alt: "A bar chart showing number of cappuccino observations taken by country."
#| fig-width: 6 
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: 100%
ggplot(cafe_plot,
       aes(x = country, # <1>
           fill = country, # <1>
           y = prop)) + # <1>
  geom_col() + # <2>
  coord_flip() + # <3>
  guides(fill = 'none') + # <4>
  ylab("Proportion of Observations") + # <5>
  xlab("") + # <5> 
  ggtitle("Cappuccino Index Data by Country") # <6>
```
1.  Show country on the x-axis, fill by country as well, then show prop on the y-axis.
2.  Create columns (rectangles)
3.  Flip x and y so that labels are horizontal and more easily read
4.  Remove the fill legend because it's equivalent to the x (now y) axis.
5.  Set axis labels
6. Set plot title.

## Rural vs. Urban

Are the categories mutually exclusive?

```{r}
#| echo: true
cafe |>
filter(
  urban + rural + suburban > 1
) |>
  select(1:5)
```

[Ok, well that's odd, but let's just work around it for now]{.fragment .emph .cerulean-dk}

## Rural vs. Urban

First, we have to rearrange the data so that density is a single variable.

```{r}
#| echo: true
cafe_density <- cafe |>
  pivot_longer(c(3:5), 
               names_to = "density") |>
  filter(value) |>
  select(country, density, ends_with("gbp"))
cafe_density
```

## Stacked Bar Chart: Rural vs. Urban

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-alt: "A stacked bar chart showing three categories: urban, suburban, and rural. Urban makes up nearly 70% of the observations, suburban makes up another 24% of the observations, and rural accounts for the remaining 6% of the observations. Some locations fall into two categories." 
ggplot(cafe_density,
       aes(x = 1, # <1>
           fill = density)) + # <2>
  geom_bar(position = "fill") + # <3>
  xlab("") + ylab("Proportion") + # <4>
  coord_flip() +  # <5>
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), # <6>
        axis.ticks.y = element_blank()) # <6>
```
1.  put all columns in the same location
2.  color by density -- urban, suburban, rural
3.  plot the bars on top of each other, then scale to 1 so that each bar is sized by the proportion of the data in that bar
4.  Set axis labels (or lack thereof for x)
5.  Flip the axes (so that the plot fits on the slide -- not actually necessary)
6.  Remove x axis text and ticks because there is nothing on the x-axis.

## Pie Chart: Rural vs. Urban

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: 100%
#| fig-alt: "A stacked bar chart showing three categories: urban, suburban, and rural. Urban makes up nearly 70% of the observations, suburban makes up another 24% of the observations, and rural accounts for the remaining 6% of the observations. Some locations fall into two categories. "
ggplot(cafe_density,
       aes(x = 1, 
           fill = density)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "fill") + 
  coord_polar(theta = "y") + # <1>
  theme_void() # <2>
```
1.  Set coordinates to polar and specify which variable is `theta` (angle). This transforms a stacked bar chart into a pie chart.
2.  Remove grid, axis text, etc.

# Numeric Distributions

## Data Wrangling

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| 

cafe_english <- cafe |>
  filter(country %in% c("Australia", "USA", "UK")) # <1>

cafe_summary <- cafe_english |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(price_gbp), median = median(price_gbp)) |> # <2>
  pivot_longer(-country, names_to="summary") |> # <3>
  mutate(summary = factor(summary))
```
1. Get only the UK, US, and Australia
2. Summarize `price_gbp`, getting the median and mean
3. Pivot longer, so that we have long-form data with the summary name as the column name. This makes plotting easier.

## ECDFs

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: An empirical CDF of the cost of a cappuccino in Australia, the USA, and the UK, with all costs represented in british pounds. Australia has much cheaper coffee than the USA and the UK, though the US has more variability than the UK in price at the lower end of the distribution; after the median, however, the US and the UK have similarly priced coffee. 
ggplot(cafe_english, aes(x = price_gbp, color = country)) + 
  stat_ecdf(geom = "step") 
```

- Shows all of the data in the distribution
- Continuous variables will look relatively smooth for large enough $n$
- Discrete variables will have "steps"
- Hard to see the mean, variability, range

## Histograms - Cost of Cappuccino

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-alt: Three histograms showing the cost of a small cappuccino in Australia, the UK, and the USA. It is clear that coffee is cheaper in Australia relative to the other two countries.

cafe |>
  filter(country %in% c("USA", "UK", "Australia")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = price_gbp, fill = country)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = .2) + 
  guides(fill = "none") + 
  facet_grid(country~., scales = "free_y") # <1>
```
1. Setting `scales = "free_y"` allows the y-axis scale to vary between the different countries, de-emphasizing the lower amount of data in Australia relative to the other two countries.


## Histograms

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-alt: Histograms of the cost of a cappuccino in Australia, the USA, and the UK, with all costs represented in british pounds. Australia has much cheaper coffee than the USA and the UK, though the US has more variability than the UK in price at the lower end of the distribution; after the median, however, the US and the UK have similarly priced coffee. 

ggplot(cafe_english, 
       aes(x = price_gbp, 
           fill = country)) + 
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, closed="left") +
  geom_segment(
    data = cafe_summary,
    aes(x = value, xend = value,
        y = 0, yend = Inf,
        linetype = summary), 
    color = "black") +
  facet_grid(country~., scales = "free_y") +
  guides(fill = 'none')
  
```

- Easy to see distribution center and spread
- Sensitive to bin width/number of bins

## Histograms

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-alt: A histogram of coffee prices in the UK only, using a binwidth of 0.05 pounds. This binwidth shows that it is uncommon to have prices which are not multiples of 0.10. 

ggplot(cafe_english, 
       aes(x = price_gbp, 
           fill = country)) + 
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, closed="left", binwidth = 0.05) + 
  geom_segment(
    data = cafe_summary,
    aes(x = value, xend = value,
        y = 0, yend = Inf,
        linetype = summary), color = "black") +
  facet_grid(country~., scales = "free_y") +
  guides(fill = 'none')
```

- Easy to see distribution center and spread
- Sensitive to bin width/number of bins
  - Extra-sensitive if data are discrete or rounded

## Density Plots

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: A density plot of coffee prices in the US, UK, and Australia. 

ggplot(cafe_english, 
       aes(x = price_gbp, 
           color = country)) + 
  geom_density(adjust = 2) 
```

- Smoothed out version of a histogram
- Masks rounded/discrete variables

## Density Plots

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: A density plot of coffee prices in the US, UK, and Australia. 

ggplot(cafe_english, 
       aes(x = price_gbp, 
           color = country)) + 
  geom_density(adjust = .5) 
```
- Smoothed out version of a histogram
- Masks rounded/discrete variables
- With smaller bandwidth/adjustment, discrete variables look like zigzags.
- Adjust bandwidth using `geom_density(adjust=XXX)`
  - Try values of XXX of 0.5, 1.5 to start

## Box Plots

::::: columns
::: column
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: true
#| out-width: 100%

ggplot(cafe_english, 
       aes(x = country, 
           y = price_gbp)) + 
  geom_boxplot()
```
:::

::: column
- Box:
  - lower: 25th percentile
  - upper: 75th percentile
  - middle: median, 50th percentile
- Whiskers:
  - smallest observation that is greater than or equal to (lower hinge - 1.5 \* (upper - lower))
  - largest observation that is less than or equal to (upper hinge + 1.5 \* (upper - lower))
- Outliers: anything not covered by the whiskers are shown as individual points
:::
:::::

## Violin Plots

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: true
#| out-width: 100%
#| output-location: column

ggplot(
  cafe_english, 
  aes(x = country, 
      y = price_gbp, 
      fill = country)) + 
  geom_violin(adjust = 0.75) + 
  geom_boxplot(
    width=.1, 
    fill = "white",
    outliers = FALSE) + 
  guides(fill = "none")
```

- Density curve plotted vertically, then mirrored
- Often shown with a boxplot (or quantile lines) overlaid on top
